blocks.text: Why the altars of the idols are said to be ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai], like tortoises, in the Greek version of Os. XII, 12. And on the chelonis of Holofernes, Iudith. XIV, 13.

No word is better known to the Hebrews than גל gal, for a heap of stones. From it Galaad, a very famous mountain in the land of Canaan, took its name, Gen. XXXI, 48. So too Gallim, a town near Accaron, on which see 1 Sam. XXV, 44. Es. X, 30. [col. 1091] and Eusebius and Jerome in the Places. When Achan had been stoned because he had taken from the devoted things, a great גל gal of stones (that is, a heap) was piled over him as a memorial of the deed, Ios. VII, 26. Likewise over the corpse of the rebel Absalom, 2 Sam. XVIII, 17. Houses, too, and cities that are demolished are said to be reduced לגל, to a gal (that is, a heap), Es. XXV, 2. or לגלים, to gallim (that is, heaps), Iob. XV, 28. and Ierem. IX, 11. and LI, 37. And to become גלים נצים gallim nitsim (that is, desolate heaps), 2 Reg. XIX, 25. There is therefore nothing obscure in these words of Os. XII, 11. (var. 12.): Their altars are כגלים, like gallim (or heaps of stones) on the furrows of the field. The Prophet is speaking of the altars which the idolaters of Gilgal had built to their gods not only in the city but also in the neighbouring fields; and he compares them with the heaps of stones customarily piled up by those who clear stony fields. The Greek translators, however, for whom גל gal is elsewhere βουνὸς [bounos], a mound, χῶμα [chōma] an embankment, σωρὸς [sōros] a heap, συναγωγὴ λίθων [synagōgē lithōn] a collection of stones, render the plural גלים gallim in this passage of Hosea quite differently, namely as χελώνας [chelōnas], tortoises. Τὰ θυσιαστήρια αὐτῶν [Ta thysiastēria autōn] (they say), ὡς χελῶναι ἐπὶ χέρσον ἀγροῦ [hōs chelōnai epi cherson agrou], Their altars are like tortoises on the waste of the field. And on these words [II, 521] Theodoret observes that the tortoise, when swimming in the water, escapes the hands of fishermen more easily, whereas when walking on land it is πρόχειρος, καὶ εὐάλωτως [procheiros, kai eualōtōs], ready to hand and easily caught; so it would come about that the altars of the Gilgalites would easily be taken and overthrown by their enemies. Jerome preferred to apply what is said of the altars to the heretics, who, like tortoises, are slow of step and move about in one place, etc. Wiser than these, perhaps, will seem Cyril, for whom χελῶναι [chelōnai] in this passage are not animals but αἱ τῶν χωμάτων ἐγέρσεις [hai tōn chōmatōn egerseis], the raising of embankments; just as for Drusius too tortoises signify γεωλόφους [geōlophous], mounds of earth. And I would gladly agree with them if any example of a similar expression were given. But since none is adduced, I have two conjectures. The first is that instead of ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai] we should read ὡς κολῶναι [hōs kolōnai], a word often used for mounds. As in the Iliad, β΄ [book 2], line 811.
Ἔστι δέ τις προπάροιθε πόλεως αἰπεῖα κολώνη, [Esti de tis propároithe poleōs aipeia kolōnē,]
Now there is near the city a certain lofty mound. And in Apollonius' Argonautica, book 1, line 1114.
Φαίνετο δ᾽ ἠερόεν στόμα Βοσπόρου, ἠδὲ κολῶναι Μύσιαι. — — — — — — [Phaineto d' ēeroen stoma Bosporou, ēde kolōnai Mysiai.]
